title: Metatheory
body:
**Metatheory** asks questions about a formal system itself, where every earlier section asked
questions inside one. The system stops being the tool and becomes the object of study.

Two properties relate what a system proves to what is actually valid:

```
soundness      everything provable is valid       the system proves nothing false
completeness   everything valid is provable       the system misses nothing true
```

Both hold for sentential logic and for first-order logic, which is why a
[[Natural Deduction]] derivation and a [[Truth Table]] always agree, and why
searching for a proof is a reasonable way to spend time: if the argument is valid, a proof
exists.

The word soundness is used differently here than in [[Soundness]], where it describes an
argument with true premises. Here it describes a system.

This course states the results and stops. [[Godel's Theorem]] is what happens when the
same questions are put to a system strong enough to describe arithmetic, where completeness
fails and no consistent system of that strength proves every truth about numbers.
[[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] carries that story, alongside
[[Systems of Logic]] in [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]].
